CausalChain: Green tea catechin intake -> metal ion chelation and redox modulation -> inhibition of NF-κB/MAPK/EGFR pathways -> induction of epigenetic modifications (DNA methylation, histone modifications, microRNA regulation) -> reprogramming of cancer stem cells -> increased apoptosis and chemosensitivity
Hypothesis: Green tea catechins, especially EGCG, serve as epigenetic modifiers that reprogram cancer stem cells via redox and metal-ion mediated signaling pathways, converting them to a less aggressive phenotype and enhancing their sensitivity to apoptosis and chemotherapeutic treatments.
Abstract: We propose that green tea catechins, particularly EGCG, function not only as antioxidants but also as potent epigenetic modulators within the tumor microenvironment. In this hypothesis, chronic low-dose catechin exposure is suggested to chelate metal ions and modulate redox signaling, leading to the inhibition of key survival and proliferative signaling pathways such as NF-κB, MAPK, and EGFR. These changes are proposed to trigger downstream epigenetic modifications—including altered DNA methylation, histone modifications, and microRNA expression—that reprogram cancer stem cells from a highly aggressive, chemoresistant state to a more differentiated and apoptosis-prone phenotype. As a consequence, the reprogrammed cancer stem cells may exhibit increased sensitivity to standard chemotherapeutic agents, thereby potentially enhancing overall treatment efficacy.
